newsitem.title: USA: A few FOMC members wanted bigger March rate rise.
newsitem.headline: A few FOMC members wanted bigger March rate rise.

text.p: The Federal Reserve voted unanimously at its March 25 meeting to raise the federal funds rate by a quarter percentage point, though a few policymakers would have preferred a bigger increase, minutes issued on Thursday showed.

The policymaking Federal Open Market Committee also agreed unanimously to adopt a symmetric directive that did not bias policy toward either tightening or loosening during the period leading up to its next meeting on May 20.
At that meeting on Tuesday, the FOMC left rates unchanged.
According to the minutes of the March 25 meeting, all the FOMC members saw a clear need for a preemptive rate increase to head off any pickup in inflation.
They also agreed that the higher rates would pose little risk to the economic expansion and instead would help sustain it by keeping price rises in check.
"A few members argued that a more substantial tightening was needed," the minutes said. "In their view, a more vigorous action would lessen the need for tightening in the future."
However, other members urged a more cautious approach, given the uncertain outlook for the economy and inflation.
The members also initially split over whether to bias policy toward higher rates during the period leading up to the May 20 meeting.
A majority favored a symmetric directive.

"While additional policy tightening might be needed at some point, it did not appear very likely that developments during the intermeeting period would require a further policy move," the minutes said, explaining the majority view.
Other members argued for biasing policy toward higher rates, saying that economic growth was not likely to slow enough to alleviate potential inflationary pressures.
Nevertheless, the FOMC members acknowledged that inflation had remained "remarkably subdued" and that any increase in inflationary pressures was likely to occur only slowly.

In their forecast prepared for the March 25 FOMC meeting, Fed staff predicted that growth would slow in coming quarters to a pace "somewhat above that of the economy's estimated potential" before moderating a bit more in 1998.

Some Fed officials believe the economy's long-term economic growth potential is in the neighborhood of 2 to 2-1/2 percent a year. The economy grew at an annualized rate of 5.6 percent in the first quarter this year.

In discussing the economic outlook, FOMC members agreed that consumer spending would continue to provide a major impetus to the ongoing economic expansion, though it might diminish as jobs and income growth slowed.
"A number of members expressed the view, however, that the risks to such a forecast were in the direction of more robust consumer spending," the minutes said.
Capital spending and housing construction were also seen as slowing in coming months, though not dramatically.
